To turn a blind eye means to deliberately pretend not to notice something, especially something wrong, unfair, or troubling — even though you are fully aware of it.

The key word here is deliberately. This is not about accidentally missing something. When someone turns a blind eye, they know something is happening, but they choose to act as if they don't. They look away on purpose.

Think of it this way: imagine you see your friend copying answers during a test. You notice it clearly. But instead of reporting it or saying something, you simply look down at your own paper and say nothing. You have just turned a blind eye.
Breaking It Down Word by Word

To really understand an idiom, it helps to look at the words themselves.

"Blind eye" — An eye that cannot see. A blind eye, literally, sees nothing.

"Turn" — To direct something in a different direction.

So when you turn your blind eye toward something, you are pointing your non-seeing eye at it — which means you are making sure you do not see it. You are choosing blindness. You are choosing ignorance. Even though you are not actually blind, you act as though you are.

This idiom almost always carries a negative or critical tone. When we say someone turned a blind eye, we are usually suggesting that they should have done something but didn't. There is a sense of:

  • Responsibility ignored
  • Cowardice or convenience
  • Silent approval of something wrong

For example, if a security guard turns a blind eye to shoplifting, it means they saw it but did nothing — and that reflects badly on them. They had a duty to act, and they chose not to.

However, in rare cases, turning a blind eye can be described in a more neutral or even positive way — for instance, when a parent "turns a blind eye" to a child's small, harmless mischief. Even then, the underlying meaning stays the same: they noticed but chose not to react.

This idiom has one of the most dramatic and well-documented origins in the English language.

It comes from Admiral Horatio Nelson, one of Britain's greatest naval commanders, during the Battle of Copenhagen in 1801.

During the battle, Nelson's superior officer, Admiral Sir Hyde Parker, sent a signal through flags ordering Nelson to stop the attack and withdraw. Nelson, however, was winning the battle and did not want to retreat.

Nelson had lost the sight in one of his eyes years earlier in a previous battle. So, in a moment of deliberate defiance, he raised his telescope to his blind eye, looked toward the signal, and said something along the lines of:

"I really do not see the signal."

He then continued fighting — and won the battle decisively.

He didn't truly fail to see the signal. He chose not to see it by using the eye that couldn't see. It was a clever, intentional act of ignoring an order.

This story became so legendary that the phrase "turn a blind eye" entered the English language and has been used ever since.

The structure of the phrase:

The most common way to use it is:

turn a blind eye to [something]

The word "to" connects the idiom to whatever is being ignored. Here are some patterns:

  • Turn a blind eye to corruption
  • Turn a blind eye to the problem
  • Turned a blind eye to what was happening

You can also say "turn a blind eye on" something, though "to" is far more common.

Here are examples across different situations so you can see how versatile this idiom is:

In a workplace:
"The manager knew that some employees were arriving late every day, but he turned a blind eye to it because they were his friends."

In politics and law:
"For years, the authorities turned a blind eye to the illegal dumping of waste in the river."

In everyday life:
"Her neighbors knew the old man next door was struggling, but they turned a blind eye and never offered any help."

In history and journalism:
"Many people turned a blind eye to the suffering of refugees, choosing not to get involved."

In a lighter context:
"She turned a blind eye to her son's habit of sneaking extra cookies, thinking it wasn't worth the argument."

It's important to know what this idiom does not mean, so you don't confuse it with similar ideas.

It does NOT mean being genuinely unaware.
If someone truly did not know something was happening, you would not say they turned a blind eye. The word "turn" implies a deliberate action. Ignorance by accident is not the same as ignorance by choice.

It is NOT the same as forgiving someone.
Forgiving means you acknowledged something and consciously let it go with understanding. Turning a blind eye means you pretended the thing didn't exist at all.

It is NOT the same as being patient.
Patience means you see something and consciously wait for it to change. Turning a blind eye means you see something and act as if you don't.

These expressions share some meaning with "turn a blind eye" but have small differences:

"Look the other way"
Very similar in meaning. When you look the other way, you avoid seeing something on purpose. This one is slightly more casual and widely interchangeable with "turn a blind eye."
Example: "The teacher looked the other way when students whispered during free time."

"Sweep it under the rug"
This means to hide a problem or mistake so that others don't see it — often to protect yourself or someone else. The key difference is that this one focuses more on hiding something from others, while "turn a blind eye" focuses on personally ignoring it.
Example: "Instead of addressing the scandal, the company tried to sweep it under the rug."

"Bury one's head in the sand"
This means to refuse to acknowledge an unpleasant reality — often out of fear or denial. It is slightly different because it often refers to ignoring a problem that affects you, whereas "turn a blind eye" more often refers to ignoring something happening to others or something you have a duty to address.
Example: "He buried his head in the sand about his financial problems and refused to check his bank account."
The Opposite of "Turn a Blind Eye"

Knowing the opposite of an idiom sharpens your understanding of it:

"Blow the whistle" — To report wrongdoing publicly or to the authorities.
"Call it out" — To openly point out something wrong.
"Face the music" — To accept and confront the consequences of something.
"Speak up" — To say something rather than staying silent.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

ConceptDetail

What it means: To deliberately ignore something wrong, even though you can clearly see it.

Tone: Usually negative — it implies a failure of responsibility or moral courage.

Origin: Admiral Nelson pointing his telescope at his blind eye to "not see" the order to retreat — and winning the battle anyway.

Used with: The preposition "to" — "turn a blind eye to something."

Key distinction from similar phrases: The deliberate, conscious nature of the ignoring is what makes this idiom unique.

The beauty of this idiom is in its vividness. The moment you picture someone physically turning their unseeing eye toward a problem — choosing not to see what is right in front of them — the meaning becomes unforgettable.
